title: Does Caffeine Actually Dehydrate You? What the Electrolyte Science Shows
summary: Does caffeine deplete electrolytes? At moderate doses, coffee and tea don't drain sodium or potassium, and they count toward your daily fluids.
body_markdown:
Good news: Your morning cup is mostly off the hook. Moderate caffeine doesn't meaningfully drain your electrolytes and your coffee or tea still counts toward your daily fluid. Sweat is the real electrolyte drain. You lose the most on a long effort past an hour or on a hot, humid day. That's when a glass of water on the side is worth pouring.


## Does caffeine deplete electrolytes? The short answer


Research has found no meaningful loss of sodium, potassium or magnesium at up to about 400 mg of caffeine a day in healthy adults. That's good news for anyone who loves a second mug.


At moderate daily doses,[controlled trials](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131696) found sodium and potassium losses either stayed unchanged or rose only slightly. Blood sodium and potassium stayed steady too, so electrolyte levels held up in those trials.


Calcium and magnesium shifts amount to a few milligrams a day. Research suggests a little[extra calcium offsets it](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7599455) , and a splash of milk is one way to supply it. One caveat: the calcium evidence is mixed, most trials are small, and several enrolled only men.


## What electrolytes are and which ones matter


Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electrical charge once they dissolve in your body's fluids. Four of them matter most here:


-


**Sodium:** Sodium controls how much fluid sits outside your cells and helps your nerves and muscles work properly.


-


**Potassium:** Potassium holds fluid inside your cells and is needed for normal nerve signals, muscle contraction and a regular heartbeat.


-


**Magnesium:** Magnesium helps move calcium and potassium across cell membranes, which supports normal nerve impulses, muscle contraction and heart rhythm.


-


**Calcium:** Calcium builds bones and teeth, and a small circulating pool helps muscles contract, nerves fire and blood clot normally.


Your kidneys decide how much of each mineral you keep, and that's where caffeine comes in.


## How caffeine acts as a diuretic


A diuretic makes your kidneys release more water as urine than they otherwise would. Dehydrating is different: it leaves you with less fluid than you took in, a net loss. Caffeine is a mild diuretic. At typical caffeine levels, the fluid in your cup offsets that effect, so you don't end up dehydrated. It also flushes out a bit of extra sodium. Both effects come from the same switch in your kidneys, which the next section explains.


### Adenosine receptors and the kidney


Your kidneys filter blood through millions of tiny tubes, then pull back the sodium and water you need. Adenosine is a signaling molecule your body makes. In the kidney, it latches onto A1 receptors and tells tubule cells to reclaim sodium.


Caffeine fits those same receptors without switching them on. Picture a spare key jammed in a lock so the real key can't turn. With the signal blocked, the first stretch of the tube (the proximal tubule) and later segments pull back less sodium. Water follows salt, so a little more of both leaves as urine.


Researchers still debate the finer points. One review says caffeine raises the kidney's filtration rate, while the[Zhang meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25154702) authors say it doesn't. Either way, the sodium-reabsorption step drives the extra fluid loss.


### Why the water in your cup offsets it


The water in your mug offsets the small extra fluid loss from moderate caffeine.


A 2017 study of habitual coffee drinkers shows where the line falls. About 269 mg, close to three 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, caused no more fluid loss than plain water over three hours. At about 537 mg, more than five cups, fluid and sodium losses clearly rose.


The Zhang meta-analysis pooled 16 studies with a median dose of 300 mg. Caffeine added about 109 mL of fluid loss, or roughly 16%. That's well under the fluid in a single mug.


Bigger effects show up when conditions stack against you. In one trial, men drank a 750 mL energy drink with 240 mg of caffeine after 12 hours without fluids. They lost about 243 mL more fluid and 27 mmol more sodium than with drinks without caffeine. A large dose on an empty tank behaves differently from your usual morning cup.


## Does coffee or tea count toward your daily fluid intake?


Yes. Your coffee and tea count toward your daily fluid total much like water does.


The clearest test is a[2014 crossover trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3886980) . It followed 50 men who habitually drank three to six cups a day. For three days they drank four mugs of coffee daily, about 308 mg of caffeine. Then they drank the same volume of water for three days.


Total body water came out the same on coffee and water. Blood markers matched too, and blood sodium held steady. Sodium losses ran slightly higher on coffee days, which fits the kidney mechanism above.


The authors concluded coffee in moderation "provides similar hydrating qualities to water." The study has limits: all men, free-living rather than in a metabolic ward, and no decaf comparison.


The Zhang meta-analysis didn't split habitual from occasional drinkers. It did find women more sensitive to caffeine's diuretic effect than men. A 2025 study found habitual intake made no apparent difference to how well caffeinated drinks hydrate.


## Why regular drinkers are less affected


Your kidneys get used to caffeine. A[review of caffeine and fluid balance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19774754) describes a profound tolerance to the diuretic effect in people who regularly drink tea or coffee. The short-term effect shows up at doses of at least 250–300 mg in people who've gone without caffeine for days or weeks. At the amounts in standard servings, the authors found no diuretic action.


Mayo Clinic notes that a big dose all at once has more effect if you're not used to caffeine. If you drink coffee every day, your daily cups sit in the low-effect zone. The exception is the first big mug after a long break, like a caffeine-free vacation week. Then a glass of water alongside makes sense.


## Exercise, heat and sweat: when electrolytes really drop


Sweat drains far more sodium than coffee ever does. And when you move, adrenaline and related stress hormones narrow the small arteries feeding your kidneys. That turns caffeine's small kidney effect down even further.


Heat studies are mixed. Some find caffeine nudges up sweat rate or sweat electrolyte losses on hot days. Others find no change.


Your electrolytes drop faster in these situations:


-


Efforts lasting longer than an hour


-


Hot or humid weather, when sweat rates climb


-


Two training sessions in one day


-


Sweat rates near 2 liters an hour, the upper end of the typical range


## A practical hydration plan for heavy coffee drinkers


Food and timing cover most of what coffee lovers need:


-


**Spread your caffeine:** EFSA considers single doses up to 200 mg safe for adults, and big single doses drive most of caffeine's extra fluid loss.


-


**Pair water with the big ones:** Add a glass of water when you have a large dose, drink coffee after a caffeine break, or head into a long session in the heat.


-


**Cover potassium with food:** Adult needs sit around 3,400 mg a day for men and 2,600 mg for women. Real food gets you there fast.


-


**Cover magnesium with seeds and greens:** Men need 400–420 mg a day and women 310–320 mg. Nuts, seeds, beans and leafy greens carry the most.


-


**Add a splash of milk:** A review estimated 1–2 tablespoons of milk offsets caffeine's small effect on calcium absorption.


-


**Watch sodium only after big sweats:** Long, hot efforts are when you replace it on purpose.


##
FAQ


### Do electrolyte drinks have caffeine?


Some electrolyte drinks and powders contain caffeine; others are caffeine-free. Caffeinated electrolyte lines on store shelves range from about 40 mg per tablet to 100 mg per stick or bottle. Some energy-aisle sports drinks carry 200 mg. Check the label if you're stacking one on top of your morning coffee.


### How much caffeine is too much?


For most healthy adults, 400 mg a day is the common ceiling from the FDA, EFSA and Health Canada. The FDA reports toxic effects, including dangerous heart rhythms and seizures, at around 1,200 mg. If you have questions or concerns related to a personal health state, it's best to consult a health practitioner for guidance.


### Does decaf hydrate?


Yes. Decaf is water with a trace of caffeine, so it counts toward your fluid total. The FDA says decaf coffee typically has 2–15 mg of caffeine per 8-ounce cup, compared with 96 mg for regular brewed coffee. That's far below any dose linked to extra fluid loss.


### Is tea better than coffee for hydration?


Black tea and coffee both hydrate, although tea comes with a lower caffeine amount: Mayo Clinic lists brewed black tea at 48 mg per 8 ounces and brewed green tea at 29 mg.


### Is coffee after a workout dehydrating?


Your post-workout coffee counts as fluid. A 2002 review found people retained 0–84% of the caffeinated drinks they consumed, versus 0–81% for water. What coffee doesn't replace is the sodium you sweated out. After a long or hot session, pair your cup with water and a salty meal or snack.
